clinicalPearls: Pulpitis is inflammation of the dental pulp, most often a consequence of deep caries, cracks, or trauma allowing bacterial ingress
Reversible pulpitis produces sharp, short-lived pain to stimuli such as cold that settles quickly once the stimulus is removed
Irreversible pulpitis causes spontaneous, lingering, often throbbing pain that may worsen when lying down and can be poorly localised
Heat that intensifies pain and cold that relieves it can indicate an irreversibly inflamed or partly necrotic pulp
Pulp sensibility testing (cold, electric) helps distinguish vital from non-vital teeth and reversible from irreversible states
Reversible pulpitis is managed by removing the cause and placing a protective restoration, whereas irreversible pulpitis requires root canal treatment or extraction
As inflammation progresses to necrosis, pain may transiently ease before periapical infection develops
Referred pain patterns mean patients frequently misidentify which tooth or arch is affected
reference.pathophysiology: Pulpitis begins when bacterial products, most commonly from advancing caries, reach the pulp through dentinal tubules or direct exposure, triggering an inflammatory response within the rigid, low-compliance confines of the pulp chamber. Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability raise intrapulpal pressure, and because the pulp cannot expand, this compresses vessels and nerves, amplifying pain. In reversible disease the inflammation is limited and the pulp can recover once the irritant is removed. With continued insult the inflammation becomes irreversible, progressing to ischaemia, localised then total pulp necrosis, and eventual extension of infection through the apical foramen into the periapical tissues.
additionalDifferentials: Maxillary sinusitis referring pain to upper teeth
additionalInvestigations: Thermal and electric pulp sensibility testing
Percussion and palpation to assess periapical involvement
Periapical radiography to evaluate caries depth and apical changes
Bite test and transillumination for suspected cracks
Selective anaesthesia to localise the source of poorly localised pain
redFlags: Facial swelling, fever, or trismus signalling spread of odontogenic infection
Rapidly worsening pain with systemic upset suggesting progression to abscess or cellulitis
Airway-threatening swelling from infection tracking into deep neck spaces
reference.prognosis: Reversible pulpitis usually resolves fully after the irritant is treated, while irreversible pulpitis will not recover and needs endodontic treatment or extraction; treated teeth generally have a good outcome when infection is eliminated.
pitfalls: Assuming pain localisation is accurate when pulpal pain is often diffuse and referred
Treating irreversible pulpitis with a simple restoration and expecting resolution
Missing a maxillary sinus origin for upper posterior tooth pain
Interpreting a sudden reduction in pain as recovery rather than progression to necrosis
